description: I like programming oriented in robotics
summary:
MarsWalk is a decision-support tool that plans the first human walks (EVAs) on Mars with one rule checked at every step: can the crew still get home? It runs in a web browser on real NASA terrain of Jezero Crater, around the Three Forks depot where Perseverance left ten sample tubes. A Habitat Console plans the walk and a Field Tablet guides the astronaut.

Instead of drawing a route on a map, MarsWalk computes it. A HiRISE elevation model becomes slope, roughness, hazard and line-of-sight layers; every 3 m cell gets a cost in minutes of suit oxygen from a walking-effort model scaled to Mars gravity; and an optimal A* search finds the route while keeping the oxygen needed to walk back inside the suit's reserve. A live "safe zone" shows where the astronaut can still go and return with the oxygen left. When something goes wrong (solar storm, dust storm, suit failure, oxygen leak, a new obstacle, sunset), MarsWalk re-plans from the astronaut's position in under a second and explains why it chose the new destination. Each stop shows a real Perseverance photo taken nearby.

We cross-checked the model against Perseverance's real drives: given the start and end of one drive, 99.7% of the rover's path lies within 20 m of our computed route. With Earth up to 22 radio-minutes away, crews will have to decide on site; MarsWalk shows how NASA's open data can turn that decision into a plan with a known cost and a known way home. It is a hackathon prototype, not a certified safety system.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MarsWalk is a planning and decision-support prototype for astronaut walks (EVAs) on Mars. It runs in the browser on real terrain of Jezero Crater: a 3 × 3 km area around the Three Forks sample depot. It has two linked screens: a Habitat Console, where the crew inside plans the walk and injects alerts, and a Field Tablet, where the astronaut follows the route.

Reference scenario, EVA-1: habitat (placed at the landing site JPL certified for the Sample Retrieval Lander) → the ten drop zones of the Three Forks depot → the Wildcat Ridge outcrop that Perseverance sampled → habitat. MarsWalk returns a 1,432 m, 190-minute EVA (165 minutes of work) that uses 42% of the suit's oxygen, keeps a 192-minute margin above the reserve, stays inside NASA's 1,770 m walk-back limit with 100% line of sight to the habitat, and is GO from a 09:00 local start. The same EVA started at 15:00 is NO-GO: the crew would return after the 17:37 sunset.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Terrain. Our Python pipeline cuts a 1000 × 1000 grid of 3 m cells from the USGS/NASA Mars 2020 HiRISE elevation model of Jezero and computes slope and detrended roughness. A cell is forbidden at ≥ 15° or ≥ 0.6 m roughness, caution at ≥ 10° or ≥ 0.25 m: 82.7% of the area is free, 10.0% caution, 7.3% forbidden. The 15° limit is our assumption for a suited walker in Mars gravity (NASA's lunar concept of operations allows 20°).

2. Oxygen cost. The Pandolf load-carriage equation, scaled to Mars gravity (0.38 g), with the 82 kg astronaut and 104 kg suit plus tools from NASA's 2026 Mars spacesuit study, gives the metabolic power of walking; a Tobler-type speed slows down on slopes. Power is converted into "oxygen minutes" at the suit design rate of 1,200 BTU/h (352 W). Flat, smooth ground costs 0.027 oxygen-minutes per meter; forbidden cells cost infinity. Work at a stop burns oxygen at the design rate; standing tasks (airlock, refilling, sheltering) burn it at a resting rate of 600 BTU/h, the top of NASA's measured range for suited subjects at rest.

3. Suit budget. 8 h of oxygen (NASA Mars suit design case), an 18% reserve that the plan never spends (393.6 usable minutes; our assumption, sized to cover a suit failure on the way back), a 1,770 m walk-back radius (30 min at 2.2 mph, NASA ICES-2026-127) and a 1,155 Wh battery (NASA PLSS target). Every value in the suit file carries its source or is flagged as an assumption.

4. Planner. An optimal A* search (admissible octile heuristic) runs in a Web Worker. A Dijkstra "cost-to-safety" field from the habitat and the oxygen caches makes the point-of-no-return check instant anywhere on the map. At every point of the route MarsWalk checks four rules: oxygen used + oxygen to reach safety ≤ usable oxygen; walk-back distance; battery; and daylight (sunrise and sunset from the Mars Climate Database).

5. Live safe zone. From the astronaut's current position, MarsWalk computes every cell they can still reach AND come back from with the oxygen left. Both screens draw it (red = no return, amber = less than 30 minutes of margin) and it shrinks as oxygen is spent.

6. Alerts and re-planning. Four alerts, each with its own rule. A solar particle event sends the crew to the nearest radiation shelter (the habitat, or a pressurized rover we assume as a mission concept based on NASA's Space Exploration Vehicle). A dust storm sends them to the fastest safe point. A suit failure (oxygen use ×1.5) sends them home. An oxygen leak sends them home, or through an oxygen cache if home is out of reach. The planner re-plans from the current position in milliseconds and lists every option it considered with the reason it was or wasn't chosen ("Habitat ✗ not enough O2 · Cache 1 ✓ refill then home"). An adaptive mode drops the lowest-value science stop if a task runs long or the astronaut reports an obstacle.

7. Communications. A line-of-sight layer marks every cell with an unobstructed line to the habitat antenna (5 m mast, suit radio at 1.5 m, Mars curvature included): 26.6% of the area. Routes prefer cells with line of sight, but this never counts as oxygen. It is geometry, not a radio simulation, so the tablet says "no line of sight", never "no signal".

8. Radiation. The galactic cosmic ray dose uses MSL/RAD's 0.67 mSv per day measured on the surface (Hassler et al., Science, 2014). For a few hours it is small; the real risk is a solar particle event, which is why that alert triggers a shelter.

9. Infrastructure siting. Three oxygen caches are placed with a greedy k-center algorithm on the same oxygen costs, inside an 800 m operating area (120 oxygen-minutes each: a mission-concept assumption). As an extension, three weather stations are ranked with the VIKOR multi-criteria method.

10. Field Tablet. Next waypoint, compass, oxygen left against the cost of returning, dose, time, task checklists, alarms that close by themselves, how long the crew can stay at a safe spot, and the real Perseverance photo of the next stop (placed by the rover position encoded in each image ID). The console exports a mission report.

VALIDATION

- Hand check: 12 of 12 route statistics match a calculator; 87 unit tests and 19 browser end-to-end tests run on every change.

- Where did the rover drive? Of the 3,234 grid cells Perseverance crossed (sols 401–753, 8.7 km), 93.3% are free and only 0.6% forbidden on our hazard map, against 82.7% and 7.3% for the whole area. Dropping the same path shape at 1,000 random positions and orientations, only 2.4% avoided forbidden terrain that well. The rover's recorded elevations match our terrain with a 0.19 m spread.

- Same endpoints as a real drive (sols 538→543): 99.7% of the rover's path lies within 20 m of our route (median 5 m). On a second drive (sols 433→455) the paths diverge: the rover drove along the foot of a scarp, with 38.6% of its length on 10–15° slopes, while our walker route takes 8.5%. Rovers and astronauts optimize different things; the model behaves as a walking planner should.

A rover is not an astronaut: these tests check that the cost model is consistent with how a real explorer moved through this terrain, not that a route is safe for people.

BENEFITS

- A route with a known oxygen cost and a guaranteed way home, recomputed when the plan changes.

- A shared picture for the habitat and the astronaut, with the reasons behind every re-plan.

- NASA data that is scattered across orbital terrain, rover traverses, rover images, sample-depot records and spacesuit studies, brought into one planning tool.

- Every assumption is visible, so a crew can see what each number rests on.

LIMITATIONS

- One 3 × 3 km site.

- Not calibrated with suited walking on Mars.

- 3 m cells hide small rocks.

- Line of sight is geometric only.

- Constant dose rate.

- Screens sync within one browser.

- Caches and the pressurized rover are mission-concept assumptions.

- Validated against one rover's traverse.

FUTURE

- The same pipeline works for any site with an elevation model: other Mars landing sites, the Moon's south pole for Artemis, and Earth analog sites such as El Pinacate in Sonora, where Apollo crews trained in 1970.

- Next steps: two-person EVAs, radio relays, seasonal weather from the Mars Climate Database, and testing the tablet with analog crews.

- Our goal: help the first people who walk on Mars plan the walk, and always come home.

TOOLS

- JavaScript (Vite, Leaflet, Web Workers, BroadcastChannel).

- Node.js.

- Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, rasterio, pyproj, Shapely, pandas, Matplotlib, Pillow).

- GitHub and GitHub Pages.

- Capcut and Filmora

- No hardware beyond our laptops.

USE OF AI (disclosure)

We used AI assistants (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot) for coding and debugging, finding and summarizing sources, data-analysis scripts, and English writing and translation. The concept, the safety rules, the model choices and every number were decided and verified by our team (hand calculation, 87 unit tests, browser tests, validation against Perseverance's traverse). Every AI use is logged with time, person and purpose in AI_USAGE.md in our public repository. We used no AI-generated images, video or audio (the narration is a team member's voice), and no NASA branding.
